desc:
A courier starts in the top-left cell of the grid and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only one step right or one step down at a time. The value of every visited cell, including the first and the last, is added to the courier's score; values may be negative.

A turn happens whenever two consecutive steps have different directions (right followed by down, or down followed by right). The first step never counts as a turn. Return the largest score among all routes that contain at most t turns.
constraints: 1 ≤ t ≤ 20 (so a route with at most t turns always exists)
hints: A route is a sequence of moves. The score so far and the position are not enough to decide the next move: you also need to know whether another turn is still affordable.
Use the state (r, c, d, k): you are at cell (r, c), the last step had direction d (right or down) and you have made k turns so far. Store the best score for each state.

Arrive by a right move from (r, c-1): from direction right keeping k, or from direction down with k - 1 (that step is a turn). Arrive by a down move symmetrically. The start cell is seeded with both directions and k = 0. The answer is the maximum over all directions and all k ≤ t at the last cell.
editorial: The classic right/down DP forgets how a cell was reached, but the turn rule needs exactly that, so we remember the last direction, and since the number of turns is bounded we remember how many were used. Let f[d][k][r][c] be the maximum score of a route ending at (r, c) whose last step had direction d and that made exactly k turns.

Transitions: f[right][k][r][c] = grid[r][c] + max(f[right][k][r][c-1], f[down][k-1][r][c-1]) and f[down][k][r][c] = grid[r][c] + max(f[down][k][r-1][c], f[right][k-1][r-1][c]). The start is a special case: it has not moved yet, so it is given both directions with zero turns, which makes the first step free of turns whatever it is. Because a route has at most m + n - 3 turns, larger t can be capped. The state space is 2 · (t + 1) · m · n and each state needs two lookups, so the time is O(t · m · n); keeping only the previous row gives O(t · n) memory.
